primary_meaning: The great statue of Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2 is most commonly understood as a prophetic symbol of a succession of world empires, decreasing in glory (gold to clay) from Babylon onward, which will ultimately be destroyed and replaced by God's everlasting kingdom (the stone cut without hands). In the traditional Christian scheme: the head of gold = Babylon (explicitly identified in the text as Nebuchadnezzar/Babylon), the silver chest and arms = Medo-Persia, the bronze belly and thighs = Greece (Alexander and successors), the iron legs = Rome, and the feet/toes of iron mixed with clay = a divided or weakened final form of that empire; the stone that smashes the image represents the kingdom of God (often identified with Christ and his kingdom/church).
primary_basis: Daniel 2:31-45 (the dream and Daniel's interpretation; 'you are the head of gold,' v. 37-38; the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth, v. 34-35, 44-45)
Daniel 7:1-27 (the parallel vision of four beasts, standardly read as the same four kingdoms)
Daniel 8:20-21 (explicit naming of Media-Persia and Greece, used to anchor the identification of the middle kingdoms)
Luke 20:17-18 / Matthew 21:44 (Christ as the stone that crushes, linked to the stone of Daniel 2)
Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16 (stone imagery applied to Christ, connected to the smiting stone)

alternatives.meaning: Critical-scholarly ('Greek') scheme: the four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, with the iron-clay feet referring to the divided Hellenistic kingdoms (Ptolemies and Seleucids) and their intermarriages; the vision is read as culminating in the Maccabean era rather than Rome. This is the dominant view in academic historical-critical scholarship, though a minority position in traditional church teaching.
basis: Daniel 2:43 (mixing 'with the seed of men' read as Seleucid-Ptolemaic dynastic marriages)
Daniel 8:20-21 and Daniel 11 (focus on Persia and Greece, Antiochus IV)

alternatives.meaning: Dispensational/futurist reading: the legs and especially the feet and ten toes of iron and clay represent a future revived Roman empire or end-time confederation of ten kingdoms, destroyed at Christ's second coming; the stone's kingdom is the future millennial kingdom rather than the church age.
basis: Daniel 2:41-44 (ten toes correlated with the ten horns of Daniel 7:24 and Revelation 17:12)

alternatives.meaning: Ecclesial/amillennial emphasis: the stone cut without hands is Christ at his first coming, and the growing mountain is the church/kingdom of God expanding through history from the Roman era onward; the metals matter chiefly as the backdrop for the inauguration of Christ's kingdom.
basis: Mark 1:15 and Colossians 1:13 (kingdom inaugurated at Christ's coming)

alternatives.meaning: Moral/qualitative reading: the descending value of the metals (gold, silver, bronze, iron, clay) symbolizes the progressive degeneration of human government, civilization, or moral character over history, sometimes paralleled with the classical 'ages of man' (Hesiod's golden-to-iron ages); often held alongside, not instead of, the four-empire view.
basis: General observation of the decreasing value and increasing hardness/brittleness of the materials

alternatives.meaning: Historicist variations extending the iron-clay phase into the divided nations of post-Roman Europe (e.g., classic Protestant, Seventh-day Adventist teaching), with the stone as Christ's still-future kingdom; clay-iron mixture read as church-state or fragile national alliances that 'shall not cleave together.'

notes: The identification of the image as a sequence of world kingdoms is essentially universal, since Daniel 2:36-45 itself gives that interpretation ('you are the head of gold... after you shall arise another kingdom'). Disagreement concerns which kingdoms follow Babylon (Rome-terminating vs. Greece-terminating schemes), the referent of the iron-clay feet, and the timing of the stone's kingdom (first coming/church vs. second coming/millennium). Traditional church teaching (patristic through most conservative interpreters, e.g., Josephus, Jerome onward) is Rome-terminating; historical-critical scholarship largely favors the Greece-terminating scheme. LDS tradition also uses the stone imagery distinctively, but that is outside mainstream Christian consensus.
